title: How chocolate is made
text: After cacao pods are harvested, the beans are removed and left to ferment under banana leaves for about a week, which develops their flavour. The fermented beans are then spread out in the sun to dry. Once dry, they are shipped to factories, where they are roasted to bring out a deeper taste. Next, the shells are removed, leaving small pieces called nibs. The nibs are ground into a thick paste known as cocoa liquor. Sugar and milk are added to the liquor, and the mixture is stirred and heated for many hours, a process called conching, which makes the chocolate smooth. Finally, the chocolate is carefully cooled and reheated, a step known as tempering, which gives it a glossy finish.

title: How a hydroelectric dam produces power
text: A dam holds back a river, creating a large reservoir of water at a higher level than the river below. When electricity is needed, gates are opened and water flows down through a large pipe called a penstock. The falling water gains speed and strikes the blades of a turbine, causing it to spin. The turbine is connected to a generator, which converts the movement into electricity. The electricity passes through a transformer, which raises its voltage so that it can travel long distances through power lines. The water, having passed through the turbine, flows out into the river below the dam.

title: How glass is recycled
text: Used glass is first collected from bottle banks and household recycling bins. At the recycling plant, it is sorted by colour, because clear, green and brown glass cannot easily be mixed. The glass is then washed to remove labels and food, and crushed into small pieces called cullet. Any metal, such as bottle tops, is removed using magnets. The cullet is melted in a furnace, often together with sand and other raw materials, at around 1,500 degrees Celsius. The molten glass is then poured into moulds to form new bottles and jars, which are cooled slowly to make them strong.

title: How a tsunami forms
text: Most tsunamis are caused by earthquakes beneath the sea floor. When one section of the Earth's crust suddenly moves upwards, it pushes up the water above it. This creates a series of waves that spread outwards in all directions. In deep water, the waves travel very fast, sometimes as fast as a jet aircraft, but they are low, often less than a metre high, so ships may not notice them. As the waves approach the coast and the water becomes shallower, they slow down and grow much taller. Often the sea first draws back from the shore, exposing the sea bed, before the first wave arrives.

title: How a bill becomes law
text: In many parliaments, a proposed law, called a bill, is first introduced and read for the first time without debate. At the second reading, members debate its main principles and vote on whether it should continue. If it passes, it goes to a committee, a smaller group of members who examine it line by line and may propose amendments. The amended bill is then returned to the full chamber for the report stage, followed by a third reading, at which it can no longer be changed in detail. In a parliament with two chambers, the same process then takes place in the second chamber. Finally, the bill receives formal approval from the head of state and becomes law.
